newsitem.title: USA: Home decorating -- stylish yet inexpensive.
newsitem.headline: Home decorating -- stylish yet inexpensive.

text.p: Want to redecorate? Your local auto body shop, plumber or lumber yard can be a treasure trove of inexpensive decorating supplies, giving your home a professional decorator look at a fraction of the cost.
Style maker and decorator Christy Ferer says that if you have "champagne taste but a beer pocketbook" your home can still be a showplace of style, creativity and charm.
Long term solutions to home decorating need not be expensive. In fact, Ferer's goal is "to use what you already have or can have done in the cheapest way possible."
In her new book, "Decorating on a Dime" (Warner Books, $14.95), Ferer offers what she calls "quick decorating fixes that take about two to three hours but will stand the test of time."
"You're immediately in the (decorating) business if you take care of your own apartment or house," she said from her New York office.

As one on the cusp of style trends, Ferer said that home decorating is about five to 10 years behind clothing. Following on the minimilist style in clothing -- everyone wearing basic black a few years back -- similar minimilization of surroundings is now in vogue, she said.
Home decorating trend-setters are paring down the ornamentation, she said. "There aren't so many (knick-knacks) anymore," she said. "This is tired looking."

Simplified home decorating style does not mean austere, and Ferer sees a return to luxurous looking living- and bedrooms. But rather than a dozen throw pillows and an overstuffed chair, contemporary style calls for two well chosen pillows and some large house plants.
Because of the simplification of style, excitment is coming from colour, both on furniture and on walls.

By using various home-made or adapted items, decorating can cover up a multitude of sins that are very difficult or expensive to correct. For example, stenciling a design gives a wall a new, fresh look, and can save having to plaster and paint an entire room.

Framed photos personalize any space and can also hide a damaged wall. Anything can be framed, such as children's drawings, blocks of postage stamps (Ferer goes for the Elvis Presley commemorative one) or jewelry pieces placed under glass.
Striping walls is also an easy way to create a bold look, Ferer says.

One trick to solving home decorating problems without spending a lot of time or money is to use local resources. Auto body shops and dry cleaners are among the resources you never knew you had, she said.

An auto body shop is where you can get anything lacquered or sandblasted, a technique that creates an antique or weathered look for otherwise ordinary furniture. Auto body shops also carry black vinyl for car interiors, which can be used to upholster kitchen banquettes.

The dry cleaner or tailor can do straight line sewing, such as pillows, duvet covers or curtains. Using your own material, rug pieces or large bed sheets, she can stitch up in no time items that might cost you 10 times as much to buy ready made.

One of Ferer's decorating favourites is a home-made brass and glass occasional table. The brass comes from the plumbing supply store, where they can weld together the tubing to fit any specifications. A small table like this could cost about $110 to make, she said, far less than a similar style would cost at a store.

Ferer, who appears on NBC television's "Today" show, said that to save money on expensive monogrammed bathtowels or blankets, buy plain items at a local discount store and take them to a shop where they monogram baseball jackets for the local little league. They'll monogram the towels for you, at a fraction of what you might pay otherwise.
To be a home decorator, one must have tools of the trade. One of the most important, Ferer says, is Magna Tac, a clear industrial adhesive. Another is an industrial strength staple gun.
"Decorating is a state of doing," Ferer says. "Don't be afraid of your own style instincts."
